content: A dental impression is a precise and detailed representation of a portion or the entirety of an individual’s dentition, as well as other structures within the oral cavity. It serves as a negative mold of the teeth and gums, which can subsequently be utilized to create a physical cast or model of the dentition. This model is essential for the fabrication of dental prostheses such as dentures, crowns, or other restorative devices. The process of taking a dental impression involves placing a viscous liquid material into the patient’s mouth, typically using a customized tray designed to fit the oral anatomy. This material undergoes a setting process, transforming into an elastic solid. Once removed from the mouth, the impression retains the exact shape and contours of the teeth and surrounding structures. Common materials employed for dental impressions include sodium alginate, polyether, and silicones. The silicones are further categorized into condensation-cured silicones and addition-cured silicones, the latter often referred to as polyvinyl siloxane. Historically, other materials such as plaster of Paris, zinc oxide/eugenol, and agar were also used for this purpose.
